story.e:
**Years pass.** Nebuchadnezzar is no longer alive. Now **Belshazzar** is king.

*King Belshazzar made a great feast for **a thousand** of his nobles, and he drank the wine before the thousand.* (5:1)

**And then something comes into his mind.**

*Under the influence of the wine he commanded that the gold and silver vessels be brought in, which Nebuchadnezzar his father had **carried off from the temple in Jerusalem**.* (5:2)

**Do you remember these vessels?** The book **began with them.** In 1:2 we read: *he carried off the vessels of the house of God to the land of Shinar.*

Now, four chapters later, he is **drinking from them** at a feast.

*They drank, and praised the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone.* (5:4)

**And here is a hidden detail.** Look at the materials: **gold, silver, bronze, iron.** Where did we see these? **On the statue of chapter 2!** The materials of the four empires are now **the materials of the idols.**

**And then:**

*In that same hour **the fingers of a human hand** appeared and wrote on the wall of the royal palace, opposite the lampstand.* (5:5)

*The king face was changed, his thoughts terrified him, his limbs grew weak, and **his knees knocked together**.* (5:6)

He calls in all his diviners and promises something big:

*Whoever reads this writing and tells its meaning will be clothed in purple and be **third in the kingdom**.* (5:7)

**Why third, and not second?** This is very interesting, and we discuss it in detail at the next level. Briefly: because Belshazzar **was himself only second.**

*But they could not read the writing, nor could they tell the king its meaning.* (5:8)

**Why could they not read it?** That too at the next level — but the answer is very beautiful: **the words were visible; they just had no sense.**

**And then someone remembers Daniel:**

*There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of the holy God; Nebuchadnezzar your father made him chief of the magicians.* (5:11)

**Daniel is old by now.** Decades may have passed since chapter 2. But **they remembered him.**

**And now notice Daniel's first word:**

*Let **your gifts remain with you**, but I will read the writing to the king and give its meaning.* (5:17)

**He gives back the purple and the third place** before he says anything. He does not speak the truth **for payment.**

**And after this comes the most important part of the chapter — and it is not the writing.**

Daniel first speaks **about the past**:

*King, the Most High God gave kingship and greatness to **Nebuchadnezzar your father**.* (5:18)

*But when his heart exalted itself and his spirit grew hard, **he was brought down from his royal throne**.* (5:20)

**That is chapter 4** — which we read in the previous part.

**And then he states the charge:**

**And you, Belshazzar, his son, did not humble yourself, although you knew all this.** (5:22)

**Stop here.** Because this is the axis of the chapter.

The charge is **not** that Belshazzar did not know. The charge is that he **knew.**

He knew the story. He had heard what happened to his predecessor. And **still not.**

*You praised the gods of gold and silver, which **do not see, do not hear and know nothing**; but the God **in whose hand your life is**, you did not glorify.* (5:23)

**Notice the contrast.** He does not say that the idols are **evil** or **strong.** He says that they **know nothing.** And that the real God is the one **in whose hand your life is.**

**And now the writing:**

*And this is the writing that stands there: **mene, mene, teqel, upharsin**.* (5:25)

*Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and **brought it to an end**.* (5:26)

*Teqel: **you were weighed on the scales and found light**.* (5:27)

*Peres: your kingdom has been divided and given to **the Medes and the Persians**.* (5:28)

**And the chapter's last verse:**

*That very night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed.* (5:30)

**That very night.** The feast was still going on.
story.m:
**Where are we?** This is the fifth part on the book of Daniel (p28). In chapter 4 (p27), the humbling and restoration of Nebuchadnezzar. Now **chapter 5**, and this chapter **directly uses** chapter 4: Daniel says to Belshazzar in so many words that *you knew all this* (5:22).

**The frame that now closes: the temple vessels.** This is one of the chapter's finest structural observations.

| Place | What happens to the vessels |
|---|---|
| **1:2** | *he carried off the vessels of the house of God to the land of Shinar* |
| **5:2-3** | *let the gold and silver vessels be brought in… and they drank from them* |
| **5:23** | *you had the vessels of his house brought in* — Daniel's charge |
| (after the book) | **Ezra 1:7-11** — Cyrus **gives the vessels back** |

So the book **begins** with the vessels (they go into captivity), **peaks** here (they are drunk from at a feast), and the biblical story later **gives them back.**

**Why does this matter?** Because it shows that chapter 5 is not a new story. It takes up **the book's own opening image.**

**The list of materials in 5:4 — a hidden back-reference.** *They drank, and praised the gods of **gold, silver, bronze, iron**, wood and stone.*

Look at the first four. **Exactly the materials of the statue in chapter 2:**

| Chapter 2 (the statue) | Chapter 5 (the gods) |
|---|---|
| head of **gold** | god of **gold** |
| chest and arms of **silver** | god of **silver** |
| belly and sides of **bronze** | god of **bronze** |
| legs of **iron** | god of **iron** |
| — | gods of **wood** and **stone** |

**What does this say?** That the materials of the empires and the materials of the idols are **the same.** What the stone shattered in chapter 2 is here **praised as a god.**

This is **probably deliberate** — the book makes dense use of internal back-references (see the connection of 2:21 and 4:14).

**The third place — and a noteworthy historical datum.** *Whoever reads it… will be clothed in purple and be **third** in the kingdom.* (5:7, and the same in 5:16 and 5:29)

**Why third?** This is odd: the one who stands at the king's right hand is usually **second.**

**And here is the answer, and it speaks in the book's favour:**

By the Babylonian texts the **last king of Babylon was Nabonidus.** And for a great part of Nabonidus's reign he **was not in Babylon**: he stayed in **Teima** in Arabia, for years.

During that time **his son, Belshazzar**, exercised royal power in the capital — as a **co-regent**, not as king.

That is:
- **first**: Nabonidus (the king),
- **second**: Belshazzar,
- **third**: the highest place Belshazzar **could give away.**

**And Babylonian sources confirm this:** the **Nabonidus Chronicle** and the so-called **Verse Account** about him mention that Nabonidus was in Teima and that the crown prince carried the army and the affairs.

**What does this mean?** That the word *third* in 5:7 is **not a random number.** It is a detail that **only someone who knows** the actual Babylonian arrangement could get right — and that arrangement was **forgotten for many centuries**, because not even the ancient Greek writers knew of Belshazzar.

**And now the other side: the word father.** This too has to be said honestly.

The chapter calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's **father** in **four places** (5:2, 5:11, 5:13, 5:18).

**But historically Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus**, not of Nebuchadnezzar.

**What is the explanation?** There are four possibilities:

**1. The Aramaic word ab is broader.** In Hebrew and Aramaic *av* (father) can also mean a **distant ancestor** or a **predecessor**, not only an immediate parent. For example **1 Kings 15:11** calls David **the father of Asa**, though David was an ancestor around his great-great-grandfather.

**2. A dynastic sense.** In the ancient Near East the king on the throne could be called the **son of his predecessor** even when he was not a blood descendant — that is, *father* = *my predecessor on the throne.*

**3. A family connection.** Some suppose that Belshazzar's **mother** was a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar — then Nebuchadnezzar would be his **grandfather.** This is **not documented**, only a supposition.

**4. A historical imprecision.** Some scholars hold that the book is **not accurate** here, and this connects with the dating question (see p24).

**Do I settle it?** No. The **first two** are linguistically well grounded, the third is a supposition, the fourth is seriously held.

**And now look at the balance:** this same chapter contains a **very accurate** detail (the third place) and a **difficulty** (the word father). **Both** have to be said — whoever says only one is not reading the text but defending their own position.

**Why could they not read the writing?** This is the chapter's most ingenious question, and the answer lies in the **language.**

The four words: **mene, mene, teqel, upharsin.**

**In themselves these are weights:**

| The word | What it is |
|---|---|
| **mene** | **mina** (a unit of weight, about 500 grams) |
| **teqel** | **shekel** (a fiftieth of a mina) |
| **parsin** | **half-minas** (*peres* = half, and *-in* is the plural) |

So if someone reads the words as **nouns**, then what stands on the wall is: *mina, mina, shekel and half-minas.*

**That is a list of weights.** Not a sentence, not a message. **That is why they could do nothing with it.**

**And now Daniel.** He reads the same letters **not as nouns but as verbs**:

| The word | As a verb | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **mene** | *menah* | **has numbered** |
| **teqel** | *teqal* | **has weighed** |
| **peres** | *peras* | **has divided** |

**And the third has a second edge too:** *peres* (division) **in sound** stands very close to the word *paras*, which means: **Persia.**

So *it has been divided* and *given to the Persians* are in **the same word.**

**So this is a triple wordplay** — and that is the explanation for why the diviners could not do it: **the letters were legible, the sense was not.**

**An uncertainty it is honest to mention:** why does *mene* stand **twice**?

The proposed explanations:
- **emphasis** (doubling is emphasis in Hebrew-Aramaic),
- **a copying error** (dittography) — some manuscripts write it once,
- **two weighings**: one for Nebuchadnezzar, one for Belshazzar,
- **the completeness of the measuring**: numbered and numbered, that is, finally.

**The text does not settle it.** And the interpretation in 5:26 takes it up **only once.**

**The axis of the chapter: 5:22.** *And you, Belshazzar, his son, **did not humble yourself, although you knew all this**.*

**This verse is the core of the whole chapter**, and it is worth seeing its construction:

| Verse | What Daniel says |
|---|---|
| **5:18** | God **gave** kingship to Nebuchadnezzar |
| **5:19** | he became so great that all peoples feared him |
| **5:20** | but when his heart exalted itself, **he was brought down** |
| **5:21** | and he remained so *until he knew that the Most High rules* |
| **5:22** | **and you… although you knew all this** |

**So Daniel does not begin with what is on the wall.** He begins with **what has already happened once.**

**And the content of the charge: knowledge.** He does not say *you had not heard of it.* He says that you **had heard** — and that is **aggravating**, not mitigating.

This is one of the module's recurring thoughts: knowledge also means **responsibility.** (Cf. p22, Eccl 1:18: *whoever increases knowledge increases pain.*)

**5:23 — the sentence about the idols.** *You praised the gods of gold and silver, which **do not see, do not hear and know nothing**; but the God **in whose hand your life is**, you did not glorify.*

**Notice what it does not say.** Not that the idols are **evil**, or that they are **rivals.** It says that they **know nothing.**

This is the usual language of biblical idol-criticism — and its finest examples are **Psalm 115:4-8** and **Isaiah 44:9-20**: *they have mouths but do not speak; they have eyes but do not see.*

**And the contrast:** the real God is the one **in whose hand your life is** (Aramaic: *nishmetach*, your breath, your life).

**5:30 — and a historical question.** *That very night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed.*

Babylon came into Cyrus's hands in **539 BC.** And here it is worth giving the sources **precisely**:

| Source | What it says |
|---|---|
| **Nabonidus Chronicle** (Babylonian) | the city fell **without a battle**; it does **not** mention a feast, and does not mention Belshazzar's death |
| **Cyrus Cylinder** (Cyrus's own inscription) | he entered Babylon *without fight or battle* |
| **Herodotus** (Greek) | the Persians diverted the river, and the city fell during a **festival** |
| **Xenophon** (Greek) | the capture of the city happened **on the night of a feast**, and the king was killed |

**What can be said responsibly from this?**

**1. The picture of Daniel 5 (a feast + that same night) agrees with the Greek writers**, and Xenophon stands strikingly close to it.

**2. The Babylonian chronicle does not mention a feast** — but this is **not a refutation**: the chronicle is a short, official text, and it does not usually detail a losing king's death either.

**3. A bloodless entry and the night of a feast do not exclude each other:** the capture of the city may have been quick and unresisted while there was a feast in the palace.

**Do I settle it?** No — but the picture **fits together**, and that too is worth saying, not only the difficulties.

**And what is coming:** the next verse - **6:1** by the Hebrew-Aramaic text, **5:31** in English Bibles - reads: *and Darius the Mede took the kingdom.* **And this is one of the book's hardest historical questions** — we discuss it in the next part (p29).
story.h:
**The chapter's place in the structure.** In the concentric construction of chapters 2-7 (see p26), chapters **4** and **5** are each other's pair: both are **the judgement of a king.**

| Chapter | Who | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **4** | Nebuchadnezzar | humbling, **then restoration** |
| **5** | Belshazzar | judgement, **without restoration** |

**And the difference is the key.** Nebuchadnezzar **did not know** in advance (Daniel even gave him counsel, 4:24, and he had a year for it). Belshazzar **knew** (5:22) — and there is no counsel, no year, no restoration.

So the two chapters are **each other's opposite**, and the book states this **structurally.**

**The temple vessels — the book's internal frame.** 5:2-3 and 5:23 speak of the vessels, and this is a **direct back-reference** to 1:2.

| Place | The text |
|---|---|
| **1:2** | *he carried off the vessels of the house of God (li-mane veit-Elohim) to the land of Shinar* |
| **5:2** | *the gold and silver vessels (le-mane dahava) which Nebuchadnezzar carried off from the temple in Jerusalem* |
| **5:23** | *you had the vessels of his house (le-mane vayteh) brought in* |

**The same word** (*maneh*/*manay*, *vessel*) in all three.

**What does this say?** That chapter 5 takes up the book's **opening image**, and that the vessels are **not props** but one of the book's guiding threads.

**And the arc continues within the Bible:** **Ezra 1:7-11** lists in detail how Cyrus **gave the vessels back** — *five thousand four hundred* pieces. So what 1:2 carried off and 5:2 profaned, the biblical story **gives back.**

**The list of materials in 5:4 — a deliberate back-reference.** *They praised the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone.*

The first **four** materials are exactly the four materials of the statue in 2:32-33, **in the same order**:

| 2:32-33 | 5:4 |
|---|---|
| *dehav* (gold) | *dahava* (gold) |
| *kesaf* (silver) | *kaspa* (silver) |
| *nechash* (bronze) | *nechasha* (bronze) |
| *parzel* (iron) | *parzela* (iron) |

And 5:4 **adds two**: *a* (wood) and *even* (stone) — the **typical** materials of idol-making (cf. Deut 4:28, Isaiah 44:13-17).

**What does this mean?** Two readings are possible, and both are interesting:

**1. An ironic back-reference.** What the stone **shattered** in chapter 2 is here **praised as a god.** The materials of the statue are now on an altar.

**2. The formula of idol-criticism.** The list is established in itself: the Old Testament lists the materials of idols in several places (Deut 29:17, Rev 9:20).

**What can be said with certainty?** That the agreement of the four materials **together with the order** is noteworthy, and that the book uses internal back-references **elsewhere too** (2:21 → 4:14 → 5:21). So the irony is **probable** but not provable.

**The third place — the chapter's strongest historical datum.** The *third in the kingdom* (Aramaic: *talta be-malchuta*) appears **three times**: 5:7, 5:16, 5:29.

**Why is this striking?** Because the usual promise would be the **second** place (cf. Gen 41:40, where Joseph becomes *second*; Esther 10:3).

**And here is the explanation, which comes from the Babylonian sources:**

The **last king** of the Babylonian empire was **Nabonidus** (c. 556-539 BC). And for **a great part** of Nabonidus's reign — by the sources about ten years — he **was not in Babylon**: he stayed in **Teima** (Tayma) in Arabia.

During that time **his son, Bel-shar-usur** (= Belshazzar) carried out the royal duties in the capital: he led the army, carried the administration, and business texts swear **by his name.**

**But he was not king.** In the Babylonian texts his title is **mar sharri** = *the king's son*, that is, **crown prince.**

**So:**
- **1st place**: Nabonidus (the king, who was not there),
- **2nd place**: Belshazzar (the crown prince, who ruled),
- **3rd place**: the highest position Belshazzar **could give.**

**Which sources confirm this?**

| Source | What it contains |
|---|---|
| **Nabonidus Chronicle** (BM 35382) | notes year by year that the king was in Teima, and that the crown prince was with the army in Akkad |
| **The Verse Account of Nabonidus** | speaks of the king entrusting the kingship to his son |
| **Business and legal texts** | the title *mar sharri* beside Belshazzar's name, and oath formulas on his name |
| **Documents of the official named Belshazzar** | landholding and business affairs conducted in the crown prince's name |

**Why does this detail matter?** Because the name Belshazzar had practically **vanished from history** **until the 19th century.** The Greek writers (Herodotus, Berossus) **did not** know him; they gave **Nabonidus** or another name as the last king of Babylon.

Belshazzar's existence was confirmed **only by 19th-century** cuneiform finds.

**What can be said responsibly from this?** That chapter 5 contains a detail — the *third* place — which makes sense **only with knowledge of the actual Babylonian arrangement**, and which Greek historiography **did not know.** This is a datum **in the book's favour**, and it is honest to say so.

**And now the difficulty: the word father.** This same chapter calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's **father** (Aramaic: *avuhi*, *avuch*) **four times**: 5:2, 5:11, 5:13, 5:18. And 5:22 calls Belshazzar *his son.*

**Historically Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus.** The Babylonian texts say this **unambiguously.**

**The four explanations, weighed:**

**1. The broader sense of the Aramaic ab.** The Hebrew *av* and the Aramaic *av* do not mean only an **immediate parent.** The biblical usage:

| Place | What it says |
|---|---|
| **1 Kings 15:11** | *Asa did as **David his father*** — David was Asa's ancestor **four generations** back |
| **1 Kings 15:3** | the same of Abijam |
| **Genesis 28:13** | *Abraham your father* — to Jacob, though Abraham was his **grandfather** |
| **Daniel 2:23** | *the God of my fathers* — of the lineage |

**This argument is strong**, and linguistically well grounded.

**2. The dynastic-succession sense.** In the ancient Near East, Assyrian and Babylonian inscriptions often called the king on the throne the **son of his predecessor**, even when he was a usurper. For example the Assyrian inscriptions call Jehu *the son of Omri*, though Jehu **wiped out** the house of Omri (2 Kings 9-10).

**This too is a strong argument.**

**3. A possible family connection.** By one supposition Nabonidus married a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, and then Belshazzar would be **Nebuchadnezzar's grandson** — so *his father* = *his grandfather.*

**This explanation is not documented.** Nabonidus's inscriptions speak at length of his mother (Adad-guppi), not of his wife. So this is a **supposition**, not a datum.

**4. A historical imprecision.** Some scholars hold that the book is simply not accurate here, and this connects with the dating question (see p24): if the book's final form is much later, then the name of Nabonidus had already **faded**, and Nebuchadnezzar was **the** memorable Babylonian king.

**This too is seriously held**, and cannot be swept aside.

**So what can I say responsibly?**

**1. The difficulty is real:** blood descent **does not hold.**

**2. The first two explanations are linguistically well grounded**, and follow directly from the biblical use of *av.*

**3. The fourth explanation is serious too**, and cannot be ruled out.

**4. And the balance:** this same chapter contains a **very accurate** detail (the third place) and a **difficulty** (the word father). **Both** are part of the text. Whoever states only the accuracy is defending the book; whoever states only the difficulty is attacking it. **Neither is reading.**

**The writing — the linguistic solution.** *Mene mene teqel upharsin* (Aramaic: *mene mene teqel u-farsin*).

**1. In themselves they are weights.**

| The word | As a noun | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **mene** | *mene* | **mina** — about 500 g, 60 shekels |
| **teqel** | *teqel* | **shekel** — a fiftieth of a mina (in the Babylonian system) |
| **farsin** | *parsin* | **half-minas** — the plural of *peras* (half) |

So on the wall, read **as nouns**, this stands: *mina, mina, shekel and half-minas.*

**That is a list of weights** — not a sentence. And this is the explanation of what 5:8 says: *they could not read the writing, nor could they tell its meaning.*

**An important point of precision:** the trouble was not that they could not read the **letters.** The trouble was that they could not see the **sense.**

**2. Daniel reads them as verbs.** The same consonants (vowels were not written in ancient script) can also be read as **verbal forms**:

| The word | As a verb | Meaning | The interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **mene** | *menah* | **numbered** | *God has numbered your kingdom* (5:26) |
| **teqel** | *teqal* | **weighed** | *you were weighed on the scales* (5:27) |
| **peres** | *perisat* | **divided** | *your kingdom has been divided* (5:28) |

**3. And the third word is double.** *Peres* (division) and *paras* (**Persia**) stand very close in sound.

So 5:28 says **two things** in the same word: *your kingdom has been divided*, and *given to the Persians.*

**So this is a triple wordplay**, each member of which is at once a weight and a verb — and the third alludes to a people's name as well.

**An uncertainty we do not leave out:** why does *mene* stand **twice**?

| Explanation | What it claims | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| **emphasis** | doubling is emphasis in Hebrew-Aramaic | a frequent phenomenon, **likely** |
| **dittography** | a copying repetition; some manuscripts and the Septuagint give it once | **possible** |
| **two weighings** | one for Nebuchadnezzar, one for Belshazzar | ingenious, but **cannot be supported** |
| **completeness** | numbered and numbered = finally | **possible** |

**And a textual observation:** the interpretation in 5:26 takes up *mene* **only once.** This points toward **dittography** or **emphasis.**

**The text does not settle it.** And whoever says they know why it stands twice is claiming more than can be known.

**The axis of the chapter: 5:17-23.** This passage is the substantive centre of the chapter, and its construction is strict.

**5:17 — the refusal of the gift.** *Let your gifts remain with you.*

Daniel **first** refuses the purple and the third place, and **only then** speaks. This is the same pattern as 2:30 (*not because there is more wisdom in me*): the gift and the credit must be **separated** from what one has to say.

**5:18-21 — the historical reminder.** For **four verses** Daniel recounts chapter 4:

| Verse | Which part of chapter 4 |
|---|---|
| **5:18** | *God gave kingship and greatness* — cf. 4:14, 4:22 |
| **5:19** | the size of his power — cf. 4:8-9 (the tree) |
| **5:20** | *when his heart exalted itself* — cf. 4:27 (*I have built*) |
| **5:21** | *until he knew that the Most High rules* — cf. 4:14, 4:31-34 |

**What is Daniel doing with this?** He is not giving a new revelation. He is saying: **this has already happened once, and you know it.**

**5:22 — the charge.** *And you, Belshazzar, his son, did not humble yourself, although **you knew all this** (kol-qenema yedaata).*

**This is the chapter's most important sentence.** And its structure matters: the charge is **not** that he did not know. The charge is **the knowledge.**

**What follows from this?** That the book regards **knowledge as responsibility.** This thought appears elsewhere in the module too:

- **Ecclesiastes 1:18** — *whoever increases knowledge increases pain* (p22)
- **Job 42:7** — the friends' error was **not** ignorance but the explanation (p20)
- **Luke 12:48** — *to whom much was given, of them much will be required*

**5:23 — the criticism of idols.** *You praised the gods of gold and silver, which **do not see, do not hear and know nothing**; but the God in whose hand your **life** is (nishmetach) and all your ways, you did not glorify.*

**Two observations:**

**1. The form of the idol-criticism.** In the Old Testament this is **established** language, and its finest examples are:

| Place | The text |
|---|---|
| **Psalm 115:4-8** | *they have mouths but do not speak; they have eyes but do not see… those who make them become like them* |
| **Psalm 135:15-18** | almost word for word the same |
| **Isaiah 44:9-20** | a long satire: the idol-maker cooks his dinner with one half of the wood and makes a god from the other |
| **Jeremiah 10:3-5** | *they can do neither harm nor good* |

**And the logic is everywhere the same:** the idol is not an enemy, not a rival, not a dangerous power. **It is nothing.** What is dangerous is the **trust** someone places in it.

**2. The contrast.** The Aramaic *di nishmetach bi-deh* means: *in whose hand your breath is.*

So the real God is **not a better statue.** He is the one from whom your **breath** comes — and who did not come out of your workshop.

**5:30 — the fall of Babylon and the sources.** *That very night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed.*

Babylon came into Persian hands in **October 539 BC.** The sources:

| Source | What it says | What it does not say |
|---|---|---|
| **Nabonidus Chronicle** | Ugbaru (Gubaru), governor of Gutium, took Babylon **without a battle**; Cyrus entered **seventeen days later** | it does not mention a feast; **it does not mention Belshazzar's death** (but the chronicle is damaged here) |
| **Cyrus Cylinder** | he was let into Babylon *without fight or battle* | it does not speak of the palace |
| **Herodotus** (I. 191) | the Persians **diverted the Euphrates**, and the city fell during a **festival**, while the inhabitants were dancing and making merry | it does not name the king as Belshazzar |
| **Xenophon** (Cyropaedia VII. 5) | the capture of the city happened **on the night of a feast**, and the king **was killed** in the palace | a late work, partly a romance |

**What can be said responsibly from this?**

**1. The picture of Daniel 5 is not unique.** The feast and the night-time entry appear in **two independent Greek writers** too, and Xenophon stands strikingly close to Daniel 5 (a feast + the king's death).

**2. The silence of the Babylonian chronicle is not a refutation.** The chronicle is a **short, official** text; it does not usually detail a defeated ruler's death either — and the text is **damaged** at precisely this point.

**3. A bloodless entry and a feast do not exclude each other.** The **outer** part of the city may have fallen without resistance while there was a feast in the **inner palace** — Herodotus writes exactly this.

**4. One difficulty remains:** by the chronicle the city was taken by **Ugbaru**, not by Cyrus in person, and the next verse (6:1 in the Masoretic numbering, 5:31 in English) gives the name **Darius the Mede.** We discuss this in detail in **p29.**

**What cannot be said?** That the historicity of Daniel 5 is **proved**, or that it is **refuted.** The picture **fits** the Greek sources, and the Babylonian chronicle does **not contradict** it — it is only silent.

**What the text does NOT say.** Seven things:

**1. It does not say that Belshazzar did not know.** The charge of 5:22 is **precisely the knowledge.**

**2. It does not tell us that the words are weights.** We know that from the language — the text only says that the diviners **could not read it.**

**3. It does not say why mene stands twice.** There are four explanations, and 5:26 takes it up only once.

**4. It does not claim that Belshazzar was Nebuchadnezzar's blood son.** The Aramaic *av* is broader, but the difficulty is real.

**5. It does not say that Belshazzar was Babylon's only or chief king.** The *third* place signals precisely that he was **not** the first.

**6. It does not describe who killed him and how.** Only that *he was killed.*

**7. It does not speak of what became of the temple vessels.** **Ezra 1:7-11** tells that.

**What is next?** In p29 comes **chapter 6**: **Daniel in the lions' pit** — and the very first word of that chapter is a real historical question: *Darius the Mede.*

verse.text: And you, Belshazzar, his son, did not humble yourself, although you knew all this.

bio.hu: Dávid őt állította az éneklők élére, és tizenkét zsoltár viseli a nevét. Nem szép szavakat írt: az egyik zsoltárában bevallja, hogy majdnem megcsúszott a lába, mert látta, milyen jól megy a gőgösöknek. Nem titkolta el ezt a haragot — leírta, és úgy vitte Isten elé. Az ő énekes utódai még hetven évvel később, a hazatérés után is ott álltak és énekeltek.
bio.en: David put him in charge of the singers, and twelve psalms bear his name. He did not write pretty words: in one of his psalms he admits that his feet almost slipped, because he saw how well things went for the proud. He did not hide that anger — he wrote it down and brought it to God that way. His singer descendants were still standing and singing seventy years later, after the return home.

en.q: What did David put Asaph in charge of?
How many psalms bear Asaph's name?

hu.q: Mit vallott be az egyik zsoltárában?

en.q: What did he admit in one of his psalms?
What troubled Asaph?
o: That things went well for the proud
That he had too few singers
That he was not invited to the palace

en.q: What did he do with that anger?
o: He wrote it down and brought it to God

hu.q: Hol fordult meg a zsoltár hangulata?

en.q: Where did the mood of the psalm turn?
o: When he went into God's sanctuary
When he received a new song

hu.q: Kik énekeltek a hazatérés után is?

en.q: Who was still singing after the return home?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Istenhez csak szép és megnyugtató szavakkal lehet szólni.

en.q: True or false: we may speak to God only with pretty, calming words.
What does Asaph teach about complaint?
o: A complaint can also be prayer
Only a cheerful person may pray

bio.hu: Három fiú, akiket Dániellel együtt hurcoltak el, és még a nevüket is elvették tőlük. Amikor a király hatalmas arany szobrot állított, és a zenére mindenkinek le kellett borulnia, ők állva maradtak. A mondatuk a történet lelke: van Istenünk, aki meg tud szabadítani — de ha nem szabadít meg, akkor sem szolgáljuk a te isteneidet. Megkötözve estek a tűzbe, és a király négy embert látott benne járkálni.
bio.en: Three boys carried off together with Daniel, who even had their names taken from them. When the king set up a huge golden statue and everyone had to bow down at the music, they stayed standing. Their sentence is the heart of the story: we have a God who can rescue us — but if he does not rescue us, we still will not serve your gods. They fell into the fire tied up, and the king saw four men walking about in it.

hu.q: Mit vettek el a három fiútól a fogságban?

en.q: What was taken from the three boys in exile?
What did the king set up?
At what did everyone have to bow down?
o: At a horn blast in the morning
Ha nem szabadít meg Isten, akkor sem szolgálunk másnak

en.q: What did they answer the king?
o: Even if God does not rescue us, we will not serve another
We did not hear the music

hu.q: Mit tett a király a kemencével?

en.q: What did the king do to the furnace?
o: He had it heated seven times hotter

hu.q: Hány embert látott a király a tűzben?

en.q: How many men did the king see in the fire?

hu.q: Mi történt a hajukkal és a ruhájukkal?

en.q: What happened to their hair and clothes?
o: Nothing, they did not even smell of smoke

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: azért maradtak hűségesek, mert biztosak voltak a szabadulásban.

en.q: True or false: they stayed faithful because they were sure of being rescued.

o: A hűség nem a jó végtől függ
Csak akkor érdemes hűségesnek lenni, ha megmenekülünk

en.q: What do the three boys teach?
o: Faithfulness does not depend on a happy ending
It is worth being faithful only if we are saved

bio.hu: Zsidó ember Súsán várában, aki a szülők nélkül maradt Esztert felnevelte. Egyszer leleplezett egy összeesküvést a király ellen, és feljegyezték a könyvbe — de évekig semmit nem kapott érte. Hámán előtt nem hajolt meg, és ezért az egész népét veszélybe hozta. Nem hallgatott: gyászruhát vett, és ő üzente Eszternek a kérdést, ami az egész könyv fordulópontja.
bio.en: A Jewish man in the fortress of Susa who raised Esther when she was left without parents. Once he uncovered a plot against the king, and it was written in the book — but for years he received nothing for it. He would not bow before Haman, and so brought his whole people into danger. He did not keep silent: he put on mourning clothes, and it was he who sent Esther the question that turns the whole book.

en.q: In which city did Mordecai live?
Whom did he raise?
What did he uncover?
What happened with his reward?
Before whom would he not bow?

hu.q: Mit tett, amikor meghallotta a nép elleni rendeletet?
o: Gyászruhát vett és hamut szórt magára

en.q: What did he do when he heard the decree against his people?
o: He put on mourning clothes and ashes
He went to the palace shouting
Ki tudja, nem ezért az időért jutottál-e oda?

en.q: What message did he send Esther?
o: Who knows whether you came to this place for such a time?

hu.q: Mi lett Mordokajból a könyv végén?

en.q: What did Mordecai become at the end of the book?
o: Second in rank after the king
Ki kell mondani, amit látunk, akkor is, ha veszélyes
Mindig meg kell hajolni a hatalom előtt

en.q: What does Mordecai's story teach?
o: We must say what we see, even when it is dangerous
It is better not to speak

bio.hu: Héber neve Hadassza volt. Nem ő döntött úgy, hogy a palotába megy: elvitték. Évekig titkolta, hogy zsidó. Amikor az egész népe veszélybe került, három napos böjtöt kért, és hívatlanul bement a királyhoz, pedig ezért halál járt. Ennyit mondott: ha elveszek, elveszek. Isten neve a könyvben egyetlenegyszer sem szerepel — mégis minden megfordul.
bio.en: Her Hebrew name was Hadassah. It was not her choice to go to the palace: she was taken. For years she kept hidden that she was Jewish. When her whole people came into danger she asked for a three-day fast and went in to the king uninvited, though that carried the death penalty. She said only this: if I perish, I perish. God's name never appears once in the book — yet everything turns around.

en.q: What was Esther's Hebrew name?
How did she come to the palace?
o: She was taken, it was not her choice
She was invited as a guest

en.q: What did she keep hidden for years?

hu.q: Mit kért, mielőtt a királyhoz ment?

en.q: What did she ask for before going to the king?

hu.q: Miért volt veszélyes bemenni a királyhoz?

en.q: Why was it dangerous to go in to the king?
o: Going uninvited carried the death penalty
The throne room was far away

en.q: What did Esther say before she set out?
How many banquets did she hold before she spoke?

o: Isten neve egyszer sem szerepel benne

en.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
o: God's name never appears in it
There is no king in it

hu.q: Mit tanít Eszter története a bátorságról?
o: Félni és mégis odamenni: ez a bátorság

en.q: What does Esther's story teach about courage?
o: To be afraid and go anyway: that is courage
A brave person feels no fear

bio.hu: A perzsa király pohárnoka volt — jó állás, biztonságos élet. Amikor meghallotta, hogy Jeruzsálem falai romokban állnak, leült és napokig sírt, böjtölt, imádkozott. Aztán megrémült a király előtt, de mégis kért: engedélyt, fát, leveleket. Éjjel egyedül körüljárta a romokat, és ötvenkét nap alatt felépült a fal. Egyik kezükben a szerszám, a másikban a fegyver.
bio.en: He was cupbearer to the Persian king — a good post and a safe life. When he heard that the walls of Jerusalem lay in ruins he sat down and wept for days, fasting and praying. Then he was terrified before the king, yet he asked anyway: for permission, for timber, for letters. At night he rode around the ruins alone, and in fifty-two days the wall was finished. A tool in one hand, a weapon in the other.

hu.q: Mi volt Nehémia munkája a perzsa királynál?

en.q: What was Nehemiah's work for the Persian king?
What news did he receive about Jerusalem?
o: That its walls lay in ruins
That there was a new king

en.q: What did he do first when he heard?

hu.q: Hogyan érezte magát, amikor a király előtt szólt?

en.q: How did he feel when he spoke before the king?
o: He was terrified, but asked anyway

hu.q: Mit tett az első éjjel Jeruzsálemben?

en.q: What did he do on his first night in Jerusalem?
o: He went around the ruins alone

hu.q: Hány nap alatt épült fel a fal?

en.q: In how many days was the wall finished?

hu.q: Mi volt az építők két kezében?

en.q: What was in the builders' two hands?

hu.q: Mit felelt, amikor a gúnyolódók tárgyalásra hívták?
o: Nagy munkát végzek, nem mehetek le

en.q: What did he answer when the mockers called him to a meeting?
o: I am doing a great work, I cannot come down
Az imádság és a kemény munka együtt jár

en.q: What does Nehemiah's story teach?
o: Prayer and hard work go together

bio.hu: Pap és írástudó, aki egy egész csoportot vezetett haza Babilonból. Nem kért katonai kíséretet az útra, inkább böjtöt rendelt. Róla azt írja a Biblia, hogy szívből törekedett arra, hogy kutassa, megtegye és tanítsa Isten törvényét — ebben a sorrendben. A nagy téren hajnaltól délig olvasta fel a könyvet, és a léviták elmagyarázták, hogy a nép értse is, amit hall.
bio.en: A priest and scribe who led a whole group home from Babylon. He did not ask for a military escort for the journey; he called a fast instead. The Bible says of him that he set his heart to study, to do and to teach God's law — in that order. In the great square he read the book aloud from dawn until noon, and the Levites explained it so that the people would also understand what they heard.
